questions.q: A 28-year-old woman presents with primary genital herpes infection during the third trimester of pregnancy. What is the approximate risk of vertical transmission of HSV to the neonate during vaginal delivery?
questions.exp: Primary maternal HSV infection carries a 40-50% transmission risk to the neonate during vaginal delivery, significantly higher than the 2-5% risk with recurrent maternal infection due to lower viral loads and maternal antibodies in the latter scenario. The 70% figure represents the proportion of neonates with HSV born to asymptomatic mothers, not the transmission rate itself.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: Picture a PREGNANT QUEEN in the castle delivering triplets—FOUR babies emerge, ONE gets infected by PRIMARY herpes (40-50% risk), while THREE survive. Now imagine a RECURRING infection: only TWENTY babies out of FOUR HUNDRED get infected (2-5% risk). The THRONE ROOM displays this stark contrast in numbers.

questions.q: A 6-week-old neonate presents with erythematous, arcuate lesions distributed across the face, scalp, and periorbital regions with a characteristic appearance described as 'owl eyes.' Which maternal autoantibody is most likely responsible for this cutaneous manifestation of neonatal lupus?
opts: Anti-La/SSB antibodies targeting L-type calcium channels
Maternal IgG1 autoantibodies directed against Ro-SSA ribonucleoproteins
Anti-U1-RNP antibodies targeting the dermal fibroblasts
Anti-dsDNA antibodies crossing the placental barrier
questions.exp:
Cutaneous neonatal lupus erythematosus (CNLE) is caused by maternal IgG1 autoantibodies against Ro-SSA (present in >90% of cases), La-SSB, and less commonly U1-RNP, targeting the dermal-epidermal junction and follicular epithelium. The 'owl eyes' or 'raccoon eyes' appearance is a pathognomonic sign of SCLE-like cutaneous NLE, occurring when lesions become confluent around the periorbital areas. Anti-La/SSB antibodies cause cardiac congenital complete atrioventricular block, not cutaneous disease.
🏰 Palace: Picture an OWL perched on the ROOFTOP (Ro-SSA) of a neonatal castle, its enormous eyes glowing with IgG1 antibodies—the owl never blinks because it's stuck staring at the baby's face and scalp.

questions.q: A 52-year-old man with Wilson disease has been on D-penicillamine 1200 mg daily for 15 years. He develops asymptomatic keratotic papules in an annular, serpiginous pattern on his elbows and knees. Histology reveals transepidermal elimination of elastic fibers with a distinctive 'bramble-bush' appearance. What is the underlying mechanism of this adverse effect?
opts: Direct inhibition of collagen Type IV synthesis in the basement membrane
Interference with intermolecular cross-linking of elastin and disruption of lysine/allysine residues needed for elastin cross-linking
Chelation of zinc leading to impaired wound healing and dermal atrophy
Activation of tissue-bound complement via immune complex deposition
questions.exp: D-penicillamine causes elastosis perforans serpiginosa (EPS) through two mechanisms: as a copper chelator, it reduces lysyl oxidase activity (required for elastin cross-linking); it also chemically blocks allysine and lysine residues needed for desmosine cross-links, rendering newly synthesized elastin susceptible to rapid proteolysis. Histologically, this produces the pathognomonic 'bramble-bush' or 'lumpy-bumpy' appearance of thickened elastic bundles.
questions.hook: 🏰 Palace: A COPPER THIEF steals LYSYL OXIDASE keys from the ELASTIN CASTLE, leaving BRAMBLE-BUSH THORNS (thickened elastic bundles with lateral spikes) scattered across the serpiginous pathway—15 years of penicillamine corruption.

questions.q: A premature neonate is born through meconium-stained amniotic fluid and presents at birth with lethargy, hepatosplenomegaly, and a widespread eruption of discrete grey-white papules and pustules (1–2 mm diameter) with red margins, predominantly on the back. Which of the following best describes the pathogenic mechanism underlying this clinical presentation?
opts: Autoimmune attack on dermal-epidermal junction mediated by circulating autoantibodies against basement membrane antigens
In utero transplacental transmission of Listeria monocytogenes from a bacteremic, untreated mother, causing blood-borne dissemination and microabscesses in skin and viscera
Postpartum acquisition of Listeria during passage through an infected birth canal with subsequent CNS-predominant meningitis
Defective neutrophil chemotaxis due to an inherited genetic mutation in the HLA region predisposing to disseminated infection
questions.exp: Early-onset neonatal listeriosis (granulomatosis infantiseptica) results from in utero transplacental infection when the mother is bacteremic shortly before labor, causing widespread blood-borne dissemination to the reticuloendothelial system, viscera, and skin. The characteristic grey-white papules and pustules with red margins are pathognomonic for this condition. Unlike autoimmune bullous diseases, there are no pathogenic autoantibodies or HLA associations in listeriosis.

questions.q: Which of the following statements accurately describes the epidemiology and genetic predisposition of neonatal lupus erythematosus?
opts: NLE predominantly affects female neonates with a 3:1 female-to-male ratio and occurs exclusively in Caucasian populations
NLE has an estimated incidence of 1 in 12,500 to 20,000 live births, equal sex incidence, and is associated with specific HLA alleles including HLA-DQB1*02 and HLA-DRB1*03
NLE exclusively manifests within the first 2 weeks of life, with cutaneous lesions appearing at birth
Fetal susceptibility to NLE is independent of MHC genotype and depends solely on maternal antibody titers
questions.exp:
Neonatal lupus has an estimated incidence of 1 in 12,500 to 20,000 live births with an equal sex incidence (1:1 male-to-female ratio) and occurs in all racial groups. Fetal susceptibility is strongly influenced by specific HLA alleles, mainly HLA-DQB1*02 and HLA-DRB1*03, as well as genetic polymorphisms in the TNF-α gene promoter region. Cutaneous manifestations typically appear around the sixth week of life, not at birth, and the condition affects neonates from birth up to 3 months of age.
🏰 Palace: In the HLA castle's symmetrical TWIN DOORS (equal 1:1 male-female ratio), identical guards stand holding DQB1*02 and DRB1*03 keys—they unlock NLE in the 6th week, not week 1, opening to all racial kingdoms equally.

questions.q: A newborn with localized bullous impetigo has pustules cultured from blister fluid, and Gram-positive cocci are identified. Histopathology reveals a subcorneal acantholytic blister with dense inflammatory infiltrate. Which of the following statements BEST distinguishes bullous impetigo from staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome (SSSS) in terms of bacterial dissemination and blister composition?
opts: Both are caused by systemic exfoliative toxin dissemination from a distant primary focus
In bullous impetigo, bacteria and dense neutrophilic infiltrate are present within the blister; in SSSS, the blister fluid is sterile and lacks bacteria
Bullous impetigo affects only the dermis while SSSS affects the epidermis
SSSS presents with a negative Nikolsky sign while bullous impetigo presents with a positive Nikolsky sign
questions.exp: Bullous impetigo is a localized infection where Gram-positive cocci can be visualized and cultured directly from the blister fluid, with a dense inflammatory infiltrate of neutrophils present in the blister cavity and upper dermis. In contrast, SSSS represents generalized dissemination of exfoliative toxins from an occult distant primary focus, resulting in a sterile blister without organisms visible on histology. Both conditions share the same histopathological cleavage plane (stratum granulosum) and target antigen (Dsg1), but differ fundamentally in whether the bacteria remain localized (bullous impetigo) or act systemically from a distance (SSSS).
questions.memory: 🏰 Palace: In the BULLOUS IMPETIGO chamber, GREEN BACTERIA are partying INSIDE the blisters with NEUTROPHIL bouncers—it's LOCAL and DIRTY. But in the SSSS throne room across the castle, the toxins are INVISIBLE POISON GAS spreading everywhere from a hidden distant enemy fortress—the blister is CLEAN but the whole kingdom is SCALDED.

questions.q: A 3-week-old healthy newborn presents with multiple 1–2 mm white dome-shaped papules on the nose and cheeks. The mother is concerned about these lesions. Which of the following clinical features would help distinguish these lesions from closed comedones?
opts: Presence of a visible central punctum on the surface
Complete absence of any surface opening or central punctum
Associated with sebaceous gland enlargement
Surrounded by erythema and edema
questions.exp: Milia are completely sealed retention cysts with strictly no surface opening or central punctum, which is the key distinguishing feature from closed comedones that possess an identifiable punctum. Neonatal milia occur in 40–50% of healthy newborns on facial surfaces and resolve spontaneously within weeks to months without treatment.
questions.hook: 🏰 Palace: Imagine a sealed VAULT in the castle (milia = closed treasure chest) with NO DOOR or keyhole, while closed comedones have a tiny PEEPHOLE (punctum) you can see from the outside.

questions.q: A 28-year-old woman presents with acute-onset livedo racemosa, labile hypertension refractory to antihypertensive therapy, and a recent transient ischemic attack. Skin biopsy reveals non-inflammatory arteriolar obstruction without vasculitis. Which diagnosis best explains this clinical triad?
opts: Antiphospholipid antibody syndrome with multi-system thrombosis
Cutaneous polyarteritis nodosa with cerebral vasculitis
Sneddon syndrome
Cutis marmorata telangiectatica congenita with secondary CNS involvement
questions.exp: Sneddon syndrome is uniquely characterized by the classic triad of widespread livedo racemosa, labile hypertension, and cerebrovascular accidents (strokes or TIAs) resulting from non-inflammatory arteriolar obstruction. The absence of vasculitis on histology rules out vasculitic etiologies such as PAN or microscopic polyangiitis, and the acute presentation with hypertension and stroke makes this diagnosis more specific than APLS alone.

questions.q: A 3-year-old boy presents with onset of thick-walled blisters and erosions strictly limited to the palms and soles that worsen with heat, friction, and sweating. The lesions heal without scarring. Genetic testing reveals an autosomal dominant missense mutation in KRT5. Which EBS subtype does this clinical presentation most accurately represent?
opts: Generalized Severe EBS (Dowling-Meara Syndrome)
Localized EBS (Weber-Cockayne Syndrome)
Generalized Intermediate EBS (Koebner Variant)
EBS with Mottled Pigmentation
questions.exp: Localized EBS (Weber-Cockayne) is characterized by thick-walled blisters strictly confined to palms and soles, triggered by friction and heat, with onset in childhood/adolescence and no scarring. The KRT5 mutation and clinical distribution are pathognomonic for this subtype, making it the most common form of EBS. Generalized variants would present with widespread blistering beyond acral sites.

questions.q: Which of the following statements about HSV latency and reactivation is CORRECT?
opts: The virus remains in a latent state within epithelial cells at the primary infection site and is easily detected by host immune responses
HSV-1 establishes latency in the sacral ganglia while HSV-2 establishes latency in the trigeminal ganglion
During latency, the virus is generally not detected by host defense mechanisms and persists dormantly in regional sensory ganglia
Reactivation is triggered exclusively by immunosuppression and does not occur in immunocompetent individuals
questions.exp: During HSV latency, the virus persists dormantly in regional sensory ganglia (trigeminal for HSV-1, sacral for HSV-2) and is generally undetected by host immune mechanisms until reactivation occurs. The virus reactivates periodically and travels down sensory nerves to cause recurrent lesions, triggered by multiple factors including stress, trauma, fever, and menstruation in immunocompetent individuals.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: In the castle's CRYPT (latency), a sleeping VAMPIRE (HSV) hides from the GUARDS (immune system)—undetectable in the NERVE PASSAGES below. It sleeps in TWO TOWERS: the TRIANGLE TOWER (trigeminal for HSV-1) and the SACRAL TOWER (sacral for HSV-2). When stress RINGS THE BELL, the vampire awakens and climbs the NERVE STAIRS to cause havoc.

questions.q: A term male neonate is delivered encased in a taut, transparent, parchment-like membrane. Physical examination reveals a markedly thickened, compact, orthokeratotic stratum corneum on histology. Which of the following best explains the pathogenesis of this collodion membrane?
opts: Monogenic mutations disrupting cornified cell envelope formation or lipid processing in the stratum corneum
Polygenic inheritance with strong HLA associations predisposing to aberrant keratinization
Maternal antibody-mediated destruction of neonatal keratinocytes during intrauterine life
Perinatal viral infection triggering acute inflammatory hyperkeratosis
questions.exp: The collodion baby phenotype is driven by specific monogenic mutations affecting either cornified cell envelope formation or lipid processing within the stratum corneum. Importantly, there are no strong HLA associations because pathogenesis is strictly linked to inherited gene mutations in a Mendelian fashion, not polygenic or immune-mediated mechanisms.

questions.q: A newborn presents with severe generalized grouped (herpetiform) blisters, significant mucosal involvement, laryngeal erosions causing hoarseness, and confluent palmoplantar keratoderma. Transmission electron microscopy reveals pathognomonic clumping of tonofilaments within basal keratinocytes. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Localized EBS (Weber-Cockayne Syndrome)
Generalized Intermediate EBS (Koebner Variant)
Generalized Severe EBS (Dowling-Meara Syndrome; EBS Herpetiformis)
Junctional Epidermolysis Bullosa
questions.exp: Generalized Severe EBS (Dowling-Meara) presents at birth with severe generalized grouped blisters, significant mucosal/laryngeal involvement, and is caused by mutations in conserved regions (helix initiation/termination motifs) of KRT5/KRT14. The pathognomonic tonofilament clumping on TEM is a hallmark diagnostic finding that distinguishes this severe basal EBS subtype from all others.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: Imagine a NEWBORN in the castle being attacked by GROUPED BLISTERS arranged like HERPES (herpetiform pattern), with tonofilaments CLUMPING together like tangled ROPES around basal stone columns—the severe variant's signature move.

questions.q: Which of the following clinical features best differentiates livedo racemosa from physiological livedo reticularis?
opts: Complete resolution with rewarming and symmetric distribution
Asymmetric, irregular, branching pattern that does not completely resolve with warming and may affect the trunk
Transient appearance limited to infants and young women
Uniform cyanotic mottling in a net-like pattern that is always benign
questions.exp: Livedo racemosa is distinguished from benign livedo reticularis (cutis marmorata) by its asymmetric, irregular, branching, and 'broken' appearance, its more widespread distribution affecting trunk and extremities, and crucially, its failure to completely resolve with warming. These features indicate underlying pathologic systemic disease rather than a benign physiological vasospastic response. Physiological livedo reticularis is symmetric, uniform, transient, and completely resolves with rewarming.

questions.q: A patient with lepromatous leprosy has a slit-skin smear examination performed. When calculating the Morphological Index (MI), which of the following criteria must a bacillus strictly satisfy to be classified as 'solid' or viable?
opts: Irregular staining, beaded appearance, and fragmented ends
Uniformly bright staining, perfectly parallel sides, rounded ends, and length at least five times its width
Any stained bacillus visible under the microscope regardless of morphology
Presence of acid-fast substance interrupted at multiple points arranged in a line
questions.exp: The MI classification of viable bacilli requires four strict morphological criteria: uniform and bright staining throughout, perfectly parallel longitudinal sides, rounded ends, and length at least five times the width. Bacilli failing these criteria (irregular staining, beaded, fragmented, or granular appearance) are considered dead and non-viable.

questions.q: A premature neonate born at 35 weeks presents with a hard, armor-like shell of yellow-brown hyperkeratotic plates separated by bright-red diamond-shaped fissures. Severe ectropion and eclabium are noted. Electron microscopy shows abnormal, empty lamellar bodies in the stratum granulosum and absence of extracellular lipid lamellae. Which gene mutation is most likely responsible for this presentation?
opts: KDSR gene encoding 3-ketodihydrosphingosine reductase
ABCA12 gene encoding ATP-binding cassette lipid transporter
FLG gene encoding filaggrin
TJP1 gene encoding tight junction proteins
questions.exp: Classic Harlequin ichthyosis is caused by biallelic loss-of-function mutations in the ABCA12 gene in >93% of cases. ABCA12 encodes an ABC lipid transporter responsible for loading lamellar bodies with essential lipids and proteolytic enzymes; its failure prevents intercellular lipid bilayer formation in the stratum corneum. The electron microscopy findings of abnormal/empty lamellar bodies and absent lipid lamellae are pathognomonic for ABCA12 mutations.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: Picture a massive ARMOR-PLATED HARLEQUIN jester (>93% classic HI) locked inside a CASTLE TRANSPORTER (ABCA12) while LIPID BARRELS (lamellar bodies) sit empty on the shelves—the drawbridge (barrier) crashes open, spilling RED DIAMOND FISSURES across the courtyard.

questions.q: A term neonate born to an untreated pregnant woman with primary syphilis presents with hepatosplenomegaly, jaundice, and a maculopapular rash sparing the palms and soles. Histopathology of cutaneous lesions shows plasma cell and mononuclear infiltration surrounding blood vessels with hyperplastic endothelial cells. Which vascular pathological process is characteristic of congenital syphilis?
opts: Acute thrombotic microangiopathy with platelet consumption
Obliterative endarteritis with endothelial cell proliferation and mononuclear infiltration
Polyarteritis nodosa with segmental transmural necrosis of medium-sized vessels
Leukocytoclastic vasculitis with fibrinoid necrosis of small vessel walls
questions.exp:
Congenital syphilis caused by *Treponema pallidum* specifically produces obliterative endarteritis as its hallmark vascular lesion, characterized by plasma cell and mononuclear infiltration surrounding blood vessels with hyperplastic endothelial cells. This is distinct from other vasculitic patterns and leads to the characteristic necrotizing funisitis seen in the umbilical cord. The transmission rate from untreated maternal primary syphilis is 70–100%.
🏰 Palace: Envision a SPIRALING GHOST (T. pallidum spirochete) CHOKING and STRANGLING blood vessels (obliterative endarteritis) with MONONUCLEAR GUARDS (plasma cells/monocytes) standing watch, slowly THICKENING the vessel wall until it BLOCKS (obliterative).

questions.q: A newborn with suspected Harlequin ichthyosis undergoes skin biopsy with light microscopy. Which histological feature would be MOST characteristic of this condition?
opts: Thin, atrophic stratum corneum with absent granular layer
Extraordinarily thickened, compact orthokeratotic stratum corneum with hypergranulosis and concentric hyperkeratotic plugging around follicles
Focal areas of acantholysis with suprabasal cleft formation
Spongiosis with prominent intercellular edema and exocytosis of lymphocytes
questions.exp: Light microscopy of Harlequin ichthyosis reveals an extraordinarily thickened, compact, orthokeratotic stratum corneum with parakeratosis, prominent hypergranulosis, and striking concentric accumulation of keratotic material (hyperkeratotic plugging) around hair follicles and sweat ducts. This reflects the massive buildup of stratum corneum due to failed lipid-mediated desquamation.
questions.palace: 🏰 Palace: Imagine climbing a TOWERING FORTRESS WALL of GRANITE BLOCKS (thick orthokeratotic stratum corneum) stacked impossibly high, with CONCENTRIC RINGS of jagged armor plating around each STONE TURRET (follicles) like a medieval castle's defensive bastions—each layer thicker and more hypergranular than the last.

questions.q: A 2-day-old neonate presents with bluish-red, infiltrative papules and nodules distributed across the trunk and extremities. Histopathology reveals plaque-like aggregates of nucleated cells and non-nucleated erythrocytes within the reticular dermis. What is the pathophysiological mechanism underlying these lesions?
opts: Autoimmune destruction of melanocytes leading to depigmentation
Dermal extramedullary erythropoiesis in response to severe systemic infectious stress
Vasculitic inflammation with immune complex deposition in vessel walls
Direct bacterial invasion of dermal fibroblasts with abscess formation
questions.exp:
Blueberry muffin lesions in TORCH infections represent dermal extramedullary erythropoiesis—the fetal hematopoietic system's compensatory response to severe systemic infection. These are NOT inflammatory lesions but rather ectopic blood cell production within the dermis. The lesions are characteristic of multiple congenital infections including toxoplasmosis, syphilis, varicella, and parvovirus B19.
🏰 Palace: Picture a FACTORY (dermal extramedullary erythropoiesis) hidden INSIDE a MUFFIN (blueberry muffin lesion), frantically stamping out RED BLOOD CELLS (nucleated and non-nucleated) because the baby's bone marrow can't keep up with the INFECTION siege.

questions.q: A 4-week-old full-term infant born via vaginal delivery presents with fever, neck stiffness, and CSF pleocytosis consistent with meningitis. The mother reports consuming unpasteurized cheese one month prior to delivery. Which cutaneous finding would you most expect in this clinical scenario?
opts: Generalized petechiae and purpura with discrete grey-white pustules on the back, consistent with disseminated microabscesses
Hemorrhagic bullae and oral mucosal ulcerations with conjunctival involvement
Typically absent or minimal cutaneous involvement, with CNS meningitis as the primary manifestation
Localized vesicular eruption in a dermatomal distribution with severe neuropathic pain
questions.exp: Late-onset neonatal listeriosis is acquired during passage through an infected birth canal or postnatally and typically affects healthy, full-term infants with symptom onset weeks after birth. Unlike the early-onset form, late-onset disease characteristically presents as acute bacterial meningitis or meningoencephalitis with the skin remaining generally uninvolved in the initial clinical presentation. The CNS and meninges are the primary targets.

questions.q: During follow-up assessment of a leprosy patient on multidrug therapy (MDT), the Morphological Index is found to increase over successive visits. What does this finding most likely indicate?
opts: Excellent treatment response with effective bacterial killing
Worsening condition, treatment default, or emergence of drug resistance
Need to increase the dosage of first-line anti-leprosy drugs
Transition from lepromatous to tuberculoid leprosy
questions.exp: A steady decline in the MI indicates effective treatment response, whereas an increase in the MI suggests worsening disease, potential treatment default, or development of drug resistance. The MI serves as a longitudinal marker of bacterial viability and therapeutic efficacy.

questions.q: A 32-year-old woman presents with asymmetric, irregular, branching violaceous mottling affecting her trunk and lower extremities that does not completely resolve with warming. Laboratory studies reveal elevated anticardiolipin antibodies and a history of recurrent miscarriages. What is the pathophysiologic mechanism underlying the cutaneous manifestation in this patient?
opts: Physiological vasospastic response to cold exposure affecting cone-shaped dermal units
Intraluminal occlusion and thrombosis causing pooling of deoxygenated blood in predominantly venous areas at the margins of dermal cones
Non-inflammatory arteriolar obstruction leading to widespread cerebrovascular disease
Congenital developmental defect of cutaneous microvasculature present at birth
questions.exp: The patient has livedo racemosa secondary to antiphospholipid antibody syndrome (APLS), which causes thrombosis and hypercoagulability. The asymmetric, irregular, branching pattern that persists despite warming distinguishes livedo racemosa from benign livedo reticularis. The underlying mechanism involves intraluminal pathology—specifically, thrombotic occlusion reduces blood flow, causing deoxygenated blood to pool in the venous-rich margins of dermal cones, producing the characteristic cyanotic mottling.

questions.q: A 52-year-old woman presents with a grouped cluster of milia overlying an erythematous, edematous plaque in the postauricular region. Which rare genodermatosis would be most likely if widespread eruptive milia were the predominant feature with associated follicular atrophoderma, hypotrichosis, and multiple basal cell carcinomas?
opts: Rombo syndrome
Bazex-Dupré-Christol syndrome
Oral-facial-digital syndrome type 1
Epidermolysis bullosa acquisita
questions.exp: Bazex-Dupré-Christol syndrome is an X-linked dominant genodermatosis characterized by the classic tetrad of multiple basal cell carcinomas, follicular atrophoderma, congenital hypotrichosis, and widespread milia. While milia en plaque in the postauricular region occurs classically in middle-aged women with autoimmune/connective tissue disorders, the combination of follicular atrophoderma plus multiple BCCs specifically identifies Bazex-Dupré-Christol syndrome.
questions.hook: 🏰 Palace: Imagine BAZEX sitting in an X-marked chair (X-linked), surrounded by 4 CASTLE TOWERS: BCC's, Follicular ATROPHY, HAIR loss, and MILIA scattered like gems—a perfect deadly quartet!

questions.q: A 5-day-old neonate presents with flaccid bullae (1-2 cm) on the diaper area and neck folds, with clear yellow fluid that rapidly becomes turbid. The bullae rupture within 24-48 hours leaving thin, golden-yellow crusts with peripheral collarette of scale. Nikolsky sign is negative and mucous membranes are spared. Which desmosomal protein is the primary target of the staphylococcal exfoliative toxins in this condition?
opts: Desmoglein 3 (Dsg3)
Desmoglein 1 (Dsg1)
Desmoplakin
E-cadherin
questions.exp: Bullous impetigo of the newborn is mediated by exfoliative toxins (ETA/ETB) produced by Staphylococcus aureus that act as trypsin-like serine proteases, cleaving desmoglein 1 (Dsg1), a desmosomal cadherin responsible for keratinocyte adhesion in the superficial epidermis. The cleavage occurs at the stratum granulosum level, creating the characteristic subcorneal acantholytic blister. Dsg3 is targeted in pemphigus vulgaris; desmoplakin and E-cadherin are structural proteins but not the primary target of staphylococcal toxins.
questions.memory: 🏰 Palace: Picture a staphylococcal TOXIN (green wavy molecules) as a SCISSOR cutting through a chain of Dsg1 proteins (GOLD LINKS) at the STRATUM GRANULOSUM floor of the castle—when the links snap, the whole top layer (roof) falls away as that golden COLLARETTE.

questions.q: A 45-year-old woman with progressive systemic sclerosis has been on D-penicillamine 1000 mg daily for 18 months. She now presents with flaccid blisters on her face and trunk, along with erosions in the oral mucosa. A skin biopsy shows intraepidermal acantholysis with IgG and C3 deposits on the cell surface. Which pemphigus variant is most likely responsible for this drug reaction?
opts: Pemphigus vulgaris
Pemphigus foliaceus
Pemphigus erythematosus
Pemphigus vegetans
questions.exp: D-penicillamine is the most common cause of drug-induced pemphigus, occurring in up to 3–10% of patients after >6 months of therapy. It most commonly induces pemphigus foliaceus or pemphigus erythematosus with a 4:1 ratio over pemphigus vulgaris. The thiol (sulfhydryl) groups in penicillamine interact with desmoglein 1 and 3, disrupting cellular adhesion and increasing antigenicity.
questions.hook: 🏰 Palace: A SULFUR KNIGHT (thiol groups) strikes FOUR CASTLES (4:1 PF:PV ratio) of FOLIACEUS FORTRESSES in the dermatology dungeon—penicillamine's PF dominates the pemphigus kingdom.

questions.q: A 3-week-old female presents with peeling of her collodion membrane, revealing large, dark-brown, plate-like quadrangular scales arranged in a bark-like mosaic pattern, accompanied by severe ectropion, scarring alopecia, and extreme heat intolerance. Which gene mutation is most commonly responsible for this clinical phenotype?
opts: *TGM1* encoding transglutaminase-1
*ALOX12B* encoding lipoxygenase
*NIPAL4* encoding ichthyin
*PNPLA1* encoding a lipid-processing enzyme
questions.exp: Lamellar ichthyosis, characterized by large dark-brown plate-like scales, ectropion, eclabium, scarring alopecia, and severe hypohidrosis, is most commonly caused by inactivating mutations in *TGM1*, which encodes transglutaminase-1, an enzyme critical for cornified cell envelope formation. The other genes listed are associated with congenital ichthyosiform erythroderma, which presents with bright-red erythroderma and fine white scales rather than dark-brown plate-like scales.
